subject: Business Models
title: Dynamic Pricing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Dynamic Pricing.

hook.text: The same Uber ride costs $8 at noon and $32 during a rainstorm. The product hasn't changed.

buildup.text: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real time based on demand, supply, time, or customer data.

discovery.text: Airlines pioneered this. Two passengers on the same flight might pay $200 and $800 for the same seat.

twist.text: Amazon changes prices 2.5 million times per day. No human sets them—algorithms decide.

climax.text: Dynamic pricing maximizes revenue but erodes trust. Customers hate feeling gouged.

punchline.text: Same seat, different price. Algorithms decide what you pay.

quiz.question: How often does Amazon change prices?

details.summary: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real-time based on demand, supply, competition, and customer characteristics. Airlines change fares thousands of times daily, ride-sharing apps implement surge pricing, and e-commerce platforms adjust product prices based on browsing behavior and inventory.
details.whyItMatters: Dynamic pricing captures maximum revenue by matching price to willingness to pay at each moment. It generates billions in incremental revenue for airlines, hotels.
takeaways: Prices adjust in real-time based on demand, supply, and customer data
Algorithms optimize prices to maximize revenue at each transaction
Consumer backlash can occur when dynamic pricing feels unfair or exploitative

faq.question: How do airlines use dynamic pricing to maximize revenue?
faq.answer: Airlines adjust prices based on booking time, route demand, remaining seats, competitor prices, and customer data. Early bookers get lower prices filling capacity. Late bookers pay premiums for convenience. Business travelers pay more than leisure travelers through fare class segmentation.

faq.question: When does dynamic pricing create customer backlash?
faq.answer: When prices spike during emergencies like Uber during disasters, when identical products show different prices to different people, or when algorithms exploit urgency. Transparency about pricing rules and caps on surge multipliers help companies avoid reputational damage.
